title: Courage Under Pressure
objectives: I can describe how people respond to danger and hardship using ten precise words.
I can tell tenacious, stoic, steadfast, and defiant apart by what a character says and does.
I can use the endings -less, -ship, -ous, -ant, and -ing to understand describing words.
I can write about a person or character under pressure using evidence from actions.
rationale: Stories of survival and struggle ask students to name what pressure reveals in a person. In grade 6 the character words described habits (cautious, persistent, humble); this unit moves to qualities that appear under stress. Students sort them by what they show: how people endure (tenacious, stoic, steadfast, fortitude), what makes the situation hard (daunting, precarious, hardship), and how people respond to it (defiant, selfless, triumph). Four of the words are close neighbors, so the unit asks students to prove each choice with a detail from the text. Hostile and adverse return from earlier units as the conditions these qualities answer, and oppress as a force a person can defy.

words.def: Holding firmly to a goal and refusing to give up.
words.ex: The tenacious student rewrote her essay four times until the argument was clear.
words.ex2: A tenacious vine had climbed the entire wall by the end of the summer.
words.nonExample: Someone who quits at the first hard step is not tenacious.
words.rel: refusing to let go of a goal

apps.academic: A tenacious researcher keeps testing a question after the first results disappoint her.
apps.spoken: She's tenacious; she won't stop until she gets an answer.
apps.writing: Use tenacious for someone who holds on to a goal against obstacles.

cloze.s: Her ___ search for the lost dog lasted three weeks, and she posted a flyer on every street.

cloze2.s: The ___ lawyer refused to drop the case, even after two judges rejected it.

misuse.s: The tenacious runner gave up the moment the hill got steep.
misuse.why: A tenacious person holds on and does not give up when something is hard.

visual.alt: A flexed arm in front of a mountain.

words.frame: A tenacious person keeps ___ even when ___.

words.def: Calm and uncomplaining when facing pain or trouble.
words.ex: The stoic goalkeeper showed no emotion after letting in the winning goal.
words.ex2: Grandpa stayed stoic through the long wait at the hospital and only asked how everyone else was doing.
words.nonExample: A child who screams and sobs at every scraped knee is not being stoic.
words.rel: calm in the face of pain

apps.academic: A narrator may describe a character as stoic to show that the character hides pain.
apps.spoken: He was stoic about the news, though I could tell it hurt.
apps.writing: Use stoic for calm endurance; it does not mean the person feels nothing.

cloze.s: The ___ nurse worked through the night without complaint, never letting the long hours show on her face.

cloze2.s: Even when the doctor gave her bad news, the ___ patient only nodded and thanked her.

misuse.s: The stoic hiker sobbed and complained loudly about every small bump on the trail.
misuse.why: A stoic person stays calm and does not complain; sobbing and complaining is the opposite.

visual.alt: A stone statue face beside a calm, neutral face.

words.frame: A stoic person stays calm when ___.

words.def: Strength of mind that lets a person endure pain or difficulty.
words.ex: The young swimmer needed fortitude to keep training after her shoulder injury.
words.ex2: It took real fortitude for the explorers to keep walking into the freezing wind.
words.nonExample: Quitting the first time something hurts is the opposite of showing fortitude.

apps.academic: Biographies often praise the fortitude of people who kept working through illness.
apps.spoken: It took a lot of fortitude to finish that race.
apps.writing: Use fortitude for inner strength over a long time, not for a single brave act.

cloze.s: Climbing the last mile on a sprained ankle required remarkable ___.

cloze2.s: Her ___ during the long illness inspired every nurse on the ward.

misuse.s: He showed great fortitude by quitting at the first sign of discomfort.
misuse.why: Fortitude is strength to endure; quitting at the first discomfort shows the opposite.

visual.alt: A shield beside a climber on a rock wall.

words.def: Seeming so difficult or frightening that it makes you lose confidence.
words.ex: The stack of unfinished homework looked daunting on Sunday night.
words.ex2: Moving to a new country with no friends is a daunting step for anyone.
words.nonExample: A short, familiar chore you have done a hundred times is not daunting.

apps.academic: A daunting task becomes manageable when it is split into smaller steps.
apps.spoken: The size of the project was daunting at first.
apps.writing: Use daunting for a challenge that makes a character doubt they can succeed.

cloze.s: The tall, snowy mountain looked ___ to the first-time climbers.

cloze2.s: Writing a whole novel in one month sounded ___, but Jada broke it into small daily goals.

misuse.s: The daunting task was so simple and pleasant that everyone finished it with a smile in a minute.
misuse.why: A daunting task is hard or frightening; a simple, pleasant one is the opposite.

visual.alt: A huge snowy mountain beside a worried face.

words.def: Firm and loyal, not changing even when things get hard.
words.ex: She remained steadfast in her support of the team, even during a long losing streak.
words.ex2: The steadfast lighthouse keeper lit the lamp every night for forty years.
words.nonExample: A friend who disappears the first time you need help is not steadfast.

apps.academic: Historians describe leaders who were steadfast in their beliefs despite pressure.
apps.spoken: He was steadfast; he never doubted us.
apps.writing: Use steadfast for loyalty or purpose that stays the same under pressure.

cloze.s: Through every storm, the ___ captain refused to abandon her ship or her crew.

cloze2.s: The two friends stayed ___ in their loyalty to each other, even when others made fun of them.

misuse.s: He was steadfast, changing his mind every hour depending on who had spoken to him last.
misuse.why: Steadfast means firm and unchanging; changing his mind every hour is the opposite.

words.frame: A steadfast person stays ___ even when ___.

words.def: Not held in a safe or steady position; likely to fall or fail.
words.ex: The vase sat in a precarious spot at the very edge of the shelf.
words.ex2: After losing two big customers, the small bakery's finances became precarious.
words.nonExample: A wide, flat bridge with strong railings is not precarious.

apps.academic: Writers use precarious to describe a situation that could collapse at any moment.
apps.spoken: That ladder looks precarious; let me hold it.
apps.writing: Use precarious for a position that is physical or financial and easy to lose.

cloze.s: A ___ stack of books swayed on the corner of the desk, ready to topple.

cloze2.s: The climbers inched along a ___ ledge only a foot wide, with a long drop on one side.

misuse.s: The tower was so precarious that it was the safest and steadiest building in the whole city.
misuse.why: Precarious means unsteady and likely to fall; the safest, steadiest building is the opposite.

visual.alt: A leaning stack of bricks beside a warning sign.

words.def: Openly refusing to obey or to accept someone's authority.
words.ex: The defiant student crossed her arms and refused to hand over the phone.
words.ex2: In a defiant speech, the prisoner told the king that he would never kneel.
words.nonExample: A student who follows the rules calmly is not defiant.

apps.academic: Characters in stories may be defiant when a rule seems unfair to them.
apps.spoken: She gave me a defiant look and kept walking.
apps.writing: Use defiant for open refusal; it is stronger than simply disagreeing.

cloze.s: The ___ toddler shook his head, pushed the plate away, and said no for the tenth time.

cloze2.s: Though the guards ordered the crowd to leave, the ___ marchers stayed and sang.

misuse.s: The defiant soldier bowed politely and followed every order at once.
misuse.why: A defiant person openly refuses to obey; following every order at once is the opposite.

visual.alt: A raised fist next to a prohibition sign.

words.frame: A defiant person refuses to ___ because ___.

words.def: A condition of suffering or difficulty, such as lack of money, food, or comfort.
words.ex: The settlers endured many hardships in their first winter, including hunger and cold.
words.ex2: Despite the hardship of losing their home, the family kept their sense of humor.
words.nonExample: A comfortable weekend at the lake is not a hardship.

apps.academic: Diaries from the period describe the hardship of long journeys on foot.
apps.spoken: Walking two miles to school every day was a hardship for him.
apps.writing: Use hardship for a serious difficulty that lasts, not for a small inconvenience.

cloze.s: After the factory closed, the family faced real ___ and had to skip meals to pay the rent.

cloze2.s: The pioneers' diaries describe the ___ of crossing the desert without enough water.

misuse.s: A day of rest at a quiet beach resort is the greatest hardship a person can face.
misuse.why: Hardship means suffering or serious difficulty; a restful day at a resort is not that.

visual.alt: A shivering face beside a single loaf of bread.

words.def: A great victory or success, especially after effort or difficulty.
words.ex: Finishing the marathon after months of training was a personal triumph for Aiden.
words.ex2: The team's triumph over the league's top-ranked school came in the final seconds.
words.nonExample: A narrow loss that a team learns from may be progress, but it is not a triumph.

apps.academic: Biographies often end with the triumph that makes the earlier struggle worth it.
apps.spoken: Getting the whole class to agree was a real triumph.
apps.writing: Use triumph for a success that follows effort, not for easy luck.

cloze.s: The small town's two-to-one win over the defending champions was a ___ that people talked about for years.

cloze2.s: After months of failed experiments, the discovery was a ___ for the whole research team.

misuse.s: Losing every game of the season by a wide margin was the team's greatest triumph.
misuse.why: A triumph is a great victory; losing every game is the opposite.

visual.alt: A golden trophy with party confetti.

words.def: Caring more about the needs of others than about yourself.
words.ex: The selfless volunteer gave up her weekend to help rebuild a neighbor's fence.
words.ex2: A selfless coach thinks first about whether each player is learning, not about winning.
words.nonExample: Taking the biggest slice of cake without asking is not selfless.

apps.academic: Biographies praise people whose selfless choices helped others at a cost to themselves.
apps.spoken: That was a selfless thing to do.
apps.writing: Use selfless for actions that help others even when it costs the helper something.

cloze.s: The ___ firefighter ran back into the smoke to check that no one had been left behind.

cloze2.s: Donating her prize money to the animal shelter was a ___ choice that surprised everyone.

misuse.s: His selfless act was grabbing all the food for himself and leaving none for his friends.
misuse.why: A selfless act puts others first; taking all the food is the opposite.

passage.title: The Long Way Across Hawk Ridge
paras: The climb to Hawk Ridge looked daunting even on a clear morning. Ms. Reyes, the guide, told the eight students that the final stretch gained nine hundred feet in a little over a mile. "Nobody has to finish," she said, "but everyone has to be honest about how they feel." Ines, the youngest hiker, tightened her pack straps and said nothing. She had trained all spring, and she did not intend to turn back.

By noon the sky turned the color of slate. Wind roared across the ridge and pushed rain sideways into their faces. The trail narrowed to a precarious ledge with a long drop on one side. Ms. Reyes, who had faced worse storms, stayed stoic. She did not shout or complain. She simply checked each knot, called each name, and moved the group forward one careful step at a time.

Halfway across, Marcus, a boy who had boasted all week, stopped dead. "This is ridiculous," he said, sounding defiant and frightened at once. "I'm not going one step further." Ines saw that his hands were shaking. Without a word she took off her spare jacket and pressed it into his arms. It was a selfless act, because she was shivering herself, but she had made up her mind that no one would be left behind.

Hours of hardship followed: numb fingers, soaked boots, and a trail that seemed to stretch forever. Ines was tenacious. Whenever her legs begged her to stop, she counted fifty steps and then fifty more. Ms. Reyes, who had led groups for twenty years, called it fortitude, the strength to keep going through pain. Her own steadfast calm never wavered, and the students copied it without realizing.

At dusk the clouds tore open, and the lights of the valley appeared far below. The group did not cheer; they were too tired. They simply stood in a circle and breathed. Later, Marcus found Ines at the campfire and handed back her jacket. "Thanks," he said quietly. For Ines, the real triumph was not reaching the ridge but making sure that everyone had reached it together.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "precarious" most nearly means
choices: wide and well marked
covered in snow
difficult to find
unsteady and dangerous
qs.why: The ledge is narrow, with a long drop on one side, in a storm, so it is unsafe and unsteady.

qs.q: Why does Ines give Marcus her jacket?
choices: She wants him to stop shaking and keep going, even though she is cold too.
She is tired of carrying it.
She is afraid of Ms. Reyes.
She wants him to apologize to the guide.
qs.why: The text says she is shivering herself but decides that no one will be left behind.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Ms. Reyes is stoic?
choices: She told the students that nobody had to finish.
She had led groups for twenty years.
She did not shout or complain, and she checked each knot and called each name.
She stood in a circle at dusk.
qs.why: Stoic means calm and uncomplaining under pressure, and the passage says she did not shout or complain.

choices: the loud wind on the ridge
the strength to keep going through pain
the number of steps Ines counted
the guide's years of experience
qs.why: The text defines it as the strength to keep going through pain.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Hiking in storms is always a mistake.
Guides should never ask students to finish a climb.
Boys are more likely than girls to give up.
Real success can mean helping everyone get through a hardship together.
qs.why: Ines's idea of triumph is that everyone reached the ridge together.

constructed.prompt: Describe two characters facing the same long delay in an airport, one tenacious and one stoic. Use both words and show each with a different action.
look: gives a different action for each
shows the difference between holding on to a goal and staying calm
constructed.model: Dara was tenacious: she called three airlines and kept asking for a new flight until she got one. Her brother was stoic: he sat quietly with his book and never complained about the six-hour wait.

constructed.prompt: A student refuses to sign a petition that others are pressuring them to sign. Decide whether the student is defiant, steadfast, or both, and explain with evidence.

keeps the events in a clear order
constructed.model: Learning to swim looked daunting to Mateo. The cold water and early mornings were a hardship, but after a month he crossed the pool without stopping, and it felt like a real triumph.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for how people respond to danger and difficulty, read a survival narrative on a mountain ridge, practice five word endings, and write short character analyses supported by evidence. The close neighbors (tenacious, stoic, steadfast, defiant) are sorted by what the character actually does.

notes.va.tenacious.adj: Link to persistent from grade 6, then show that tenacious adds the sense of holding on, like a grip. Give a concrete picture: a vine, a bulldog. Distinguish from stubborn, which can sound negative.
notes.va.stoic.adj: Students may think stoic means feeling nothing. Clarify that the person feels, but stays calm and keeps going. The word also names an ancient philosophy; mention it only if the class asks, and avoid claims beyond that.
notes.va.fortitude.n: An abstract noun; pair it with a concrete action. Sort with courage (a single brave act) versus fortitude (strength over time). Practice with a ladder of endurance from short to long.
notes.va.daunting.adj: Students often use daunting for anything difficult. The key is that the difficulty makes the person doubt they can succeed. Use the family words daunt, undaunted, and dauntless to widen the word.
notes.va.steadfast.adj: Steadfast is about staying the same under pressure, usually in loyalty or purpose. Contrast with fickle. Ask for a real or fictional person who is steadfast and what they refused to change.
notes.va.precarious.adj: Works for physical position (a ledge) and for situations (finances). Use two pictures: a stack of books on a table edge and a person with a risky job. Avoid mixing it up with precious.
notes.va.defiant.adj: Defiant is open refusal. Contrast with steadfast: a steadfast person may agree with authority; a defiant person pushes against it. Use an example about a rule in a story to avoid student pressure.
notes.va.hardship.n: Can be sensitive for students who have lived through difficulty. Let students choose a fictional or historical example. Show the suffix -ship (state or condition of) with friendship and leadership.
notes.va.triumph.n: Both a noun and a verb (triumph over). The unit teaches the noun. Ask students to name a triumph that was not a win in a contest; the passage's last paragraph models that move.
notes.va.selfless.adj: Self plus -less (without). The meaning is not that a person has no self but that they put others first. Use a fictional hero to show a cost to the helper; selfless is stronger than polite.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Ms. Reyes does not shout or complain, so she is stoic. Marcus says he will not go one step further, which is openly refusing, so he is defiant. Ines keeps counting steps when she wants to stop, so she is tenacious. For each word I can point to what the character does.'
discuss: Which word in the unit would you most like to be used to describe you, and what evidence would show it?
Can a person be selfless and still need help? Explain with an example.
misconceptions: Stoic means a person has no feelings.
Tenacious and stubborn are exactly the same.
Defiant always describes a bad person.
Triumph always means winning a contest.
extend: Write a one-paragraph character sketch of a historical or fictional figure using five words from the unit.
Rewrite a calm scene so that the same character becomes defiant instead of stoic.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Return to tenacious/stoic and steadfast/defiant as contrast pairs after two days and again at one week. Revisit hostile, adverse, and oppress by asking students to describe a character facing hostile weather or an oppressive rule with two words from this unit.

A stoic person does not ___, but a defiant person ___.
wida.oral: Partner A tells a two-sentence story about someone in a hard situation without naming the quality; Partner B picks a unit word and points to the detail that proves it.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (abrumador, firme, altruista, desafiante, adversidad, fortaleza) not reviewed by a native speaker; check each against the taught sense and whether fortaleza is a fair cognate flag for fortitude.
Sense boundaries: triumph is also a verb and stoic also names an ancient philosophy; only the adjective and noun senses are taught.
Passage is a fictional hiking narrative; no real people or places are depicted (Hawk Ridge is invented).
